regimen_profiles.regimen_role: First-line metastatic non-squamous NSCLC without EGFR or ALK alterations
regimen_profiles.clinical_summary: Pembrolizumab releases PD-1 immune inhibition; pemetrexed disrupts folate-dependent nucleotide production and cisplatin damages DNA. Maintenance removes cisplatin, retaining pembrolizumab and pemetrexed.
regimen_profiles.treatment_setting: First-line metastatic non-squamous NSCLC without EGFR or ALK alterations
regimen_profiles.component_rationale: Pembrolizumab: PD-1 is a control switch on T cells, a type of immune cell. When it connects with PD-L1 or PD-L2, the T cell receives a signal to reduce its activity. Some cancers use this pathway to escape immune attack. Pembrolizumab is an antibody that blocks PD-1, helping T cells recognise and attack the cancer. It does not directly poison cancer cells like chemotherapy. Releasing this brake can also allow immune cells to attack healthy organs, which explains the different side-effect pattern and why symptoms can appear after treatment stops. Pemetrexed: Pemetrexed is an antifolate: it blocks several enzymes that cells use to turn folate-dependent materials into DNA and RNA building blocks. With fewer building blocks, cancer cells have more difficulty copying their genetic instructions and dividing. Prescribed folic acid and vitamin B12 reduce toxicity; they are part of the treatment, not supplements to omit because the drug is an antifolate. Cisplatin: Cisplatin forms links in DNA that disrupt copying and repair, helping kill cancer cells. Healthy tissues can also be affected. Kidney, hearing and nerve effects are important; blood tests, symptom checks and prescribed hydration help the team manage risk.

regimen_profiles.clinical_summary: Pembrolizumab releases PD-1 immune inhibition; paclitaxel disrupts microtubule-dependent division and carboplatin damages DNA. Maintenance removes both cytotoxic medicines, retaining pembrolizumab alone.
regimen_profiles.component_rationale: Pembrolizumab: PD-1 is a control switch on T cells, a type of immune cell. When it connects with PD-L1 or PD-L2, the T cell receives a signal to reduce its activity. Some cancers use this pathway to escape immune attack. Pembrolizumab is an antibody that blocks PD-1, helping T cells recognise and attack the cancer. It does not directly poison cancer cells like chemotherapy. Releasing this brake can also allow immune cells to attack healthy organs, which explains the different side-effect pattern and why symptoms can appear after treatment stops. Paclitaxel: Paclitaxel stabilises tiny structures called microtubules that cells need to divide. This disrupts cancer-cell division. Healthy tissues can be affected too, including blood-forming cells and nerves. That explains why infection risk, hair loss and numbness or tingling matter during treatment. Carboplatin: Carboplatin is a platinum-containing chemotherapy. Inside cells, it forms chemical attachments to DNA, including links that stop DNA strands working normally. This disrupts copying and repair and can lead to cell death. Healthy cells can also be injured, especially blood-forming cells in the bone marrow. The kidneys help remove carboplatin, so kidney function is used to calculate the dose. AUC 6 describes a target drug exposure over time; it is not a fixed dose of 6 mg.

regimen_profiles.component_rationale: Nivolumab: Nivolumab binds PD-1 on T cells. It prevents signals that can reduce the immune attack on cancer. This can also let immune cells inflame healthy tissues. It is infused every 21 days in this plan. Ipilimumab: Ipilimumab blocks CTLA-4, another control on T-cell activity. It works alongside nivolumab through a different immune checkpoint. It is given every 42 days, so it is absent from each Day 22 visit. Healthy organs can also become inflamed. Pemetrexed: Pemetrexed blocks enzymes needed to make DNA and RNA building blocks. Dividing cancer cells are affected, but healthy blood-forming and mouth-lining cells can also be injured. Prescribed folic acid and B12 reduce toxicity; do not omit them because pemetrexed is an antifolate. There are two planned doses in this regimen. Carboplatin: Carboplatin forms links in DNA that hinder copying and repair. Healthy tissues can also be harmed. Its dose depends on target exposure (AUC) and measured or estimated kidney function; AUC is not a fixed number of milligrams. There are two planned doses in this regimen.
regimen_profiles.schedule_context: The first cycle lasts 42 days: all four medicines on Day 1, then nivolumab, pemetrexed and carboplatin on Day 22. Chemotherapy ends after those two visits. From Cycle 2, nivolumab continues on Days 1 and 22 and ipilimumab on Day 1 of each 42-day cycle. Immune treatment continues while appropriate until the cancer progresses, side effects require stopping, or up to 24 months without progression. Plans can change after review.

drug_profiles.name: Pembrolizumab
drug_profiles.mechanism: Pembrolizumab is an antibody that blocks PD-1, a control switch on immune T cells. Cancer cells can use this switch to reduce immune attack. Blocking it can help the immune system recognise and attack cancer. The same increased immune activity can inflame healthy organs, which is why new symptoms need attention even after treatment ends.

drug_profiles.name: Pemetrexed
drug_profiles.mechanism: Pemetrexed is an antifolate: it blocks several enzymes that cells use to turn folate-dependent materials into DNA and RNA building blocks. With fewer building blocks, cancer cells have more difficulty copying their genetic instructions and dividing. Healthy rapidly renewing tissues, including bone marrow and the mouth lining, can also be affected. That helps explain low blood counts and mouth soreness. Prescribed folic acid and vitamin B12 reduce toxicity; they are part of the treatment, not supplements to omit because the drug is an antifolate.

drug_profiles.name: Cisplatin
drug_profiles.mechanism: Cisplatin forms links in DNA that disrupt copying and repair, helping kill cancer cells. Healthy tissues can also be affected. Kidney, hearing and nerve effects are important; blood tests, symptom checks and prescribed hydration help the team manage risk.

drug_profiles.name: Paclitaxel
drug_profiles.mechanism: Paclitaxel stabilises tiny structures called microtubules that cells need to divide. This disrupts cancer-cell division. Healthy tissues can be affected too, including blood-forming cells and nerves. That explains why infection risk, hair loss and numbness or tingling matter during treatment.

drug_profiles.name: Carboplatin
drug_profiles.mechanism: Carboplatin is a platinum-containing chemotherapy. Inside cells, it forms chemical attachments to DNA, including links that stop DNA strands working normally. This disrupts copying and repair and can lead to cell death. Healthy cells can also be injured, especially blood-forming cells in the bone marrow. The kidneys help remove carboplatin, so kidney function is used to calculate the dose. AUC 6 describes a target drug exposure over time; it is not a fixed dose of 6 mg.
drug_profiles.review_status: Source reconciled; independent clinical, pharmacy and patient/PPI review pending

drug_profiles.name: Durvalumab
drug_profiles.mechanism: Durvalumab blocks PD-L1, a protein that can reduce the immune system’s ability to attack cancer cells. Removing this signal can help immune cells act against cancer, but the immune system can also inflame healthy organs.

drug_profiles.name: Nivolumab
drug_profiles.mechanism: Nivolumab binds PD-1 on T cells. It prevents signals that can reduce the immune attack on cancer. This can also let immune cells inflame healthy tissues. It is infused every 21 days in this plan.

drug_profiles.name: Ipilimumab
drug_profiles.mechanism: Ipilimumab blocks CTLA-4, another control on T-cell activity. It works alongside nivolumab through a different immune checkpoint. It is given every 42 days, so it is absent from each Day 22 visit. Healthy organs can also become inflamed.
